Extracts the predicted NEC value as desired from an object of class bayesnecfit or bayesmanecfit.

Source: R/nec.R
nec.Rd

Extracts the predicted NEC value as desired from an object of class bayesnecfit or bayesmanecfit.

nec(
  object,
  posterior = FALSE,
  xform = identity,
  prob_vals = c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975),
  extrapolate = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An object of class bayesnecfit or bayesmanecfit returned by bnec.

posterior

A logical value indicating if the full posterior sample of calculated NEC values should be returned instead of just the median and 95% credible intervals.

xform

A function to apply to the returned estimated concentration values.

prob_vals

A vector indicating the probability values over which to return the estimated NEC value. Defaults to 0.5 (median) and 0.025 and 0.975 (95 percent credible intervals).

extrapolate

The bound beyond which the estimate is reported as censored. FALSE, the default, censors at the prediction range the fit was built on. TRUE removes the bound at both ends. A single number is an upper limit, and a pair of numbers is a lower and an upper limit, in that order. See the Extrapolation section of nec.

...

Additional arguments passed to methods. sig_val and resolution are forwarded to nsec where a finite extrapolate limit requires a curve to be re-evaluated, and are otherwise unused.

Value

A vector containing the estimated no-effect value, including upper and lower 95% credible interval bounds (or other interval as specified by prob_vals). Where any posterior draw lies beyond the range the model was predicted over, that draw keeps its rank in the summary and is given no value, so an entry falling among such draws is the end of the prediction range rather than a quantile. Attribute "censored_summary" marks which entries those are and states how many draws lie beyond each end.

Details

The NEC is a parameter in a threshold model (for example, see Fox 2010), and is a true measure of No-effect-concentration (the minimum concentration above which an effect is predicted to occur.

What is actually returned depends on the model set. Despite the function name, nec returns a no-effect estimate of whichever type the fitted model(s) support, following the convention set out in Fisher et al. (2023):

  • For a bayesnecfit holding a threshold (nec-type) model, the NEC: the nec parameter itself.

  • For a bayesnecfit holding a smooth (ecx-type) model, which has no threshold parameter, the NSEC (Fisher and Fox 2023) – the concentration at which the fitted curve falls below a reference taken from the sig_val quantile of the control posterior. This is computed when the model is fitted, using the sig_val passed to bnec.

  • For a bayesmanecfit whose model set contains both kinds, the weighted posterior mixes NEC draws from the threshold models with NSEC draws from the smooth ones, in proportion to the model weights. The result is the model-averaged N(S)EC, and a message is emitted to say so. It is not a pure NEC and should not be reported as one.

summary labels the estimate NEC, NSEC or N(S)EC accordingly, and is the better choice where the type matters, because nec always returns an unlabelled vector. Use nsec where a NSEC is wanted from every model regardless of type.

Capping and dropping

Two operations are both called censoring and they are not the same. A threshold equation's nec is a sampled parameter: a draw above the top of the prediction range has a value, and that value is known to exceed the bound, which is right-censoring in the ordinary sense. An NSEC or an ECx is read off a fitted curve: a draw whose curve never reaches the target has no such concentration in the range and may have none at any concentration, so the draw is not capped at the bound, it is recorded as lying beyond it. Both are reported the same way here, because neither claims a value for the draw.

Which quantile estimator is used depends on whether anything is censored. A posterior with no beyond-range draw is summarised exactly as it was up to version 2.1.3, with quantile's default type 7, which interpolates between two adjacent order statistics. Once any draw is censored every reported entry becomes an order statistic instead, because a value interpolated across a draw that has no value would be one the posterior does not support. Every entry therefore changes a little when the first draw is censored, including entries at the other end of the interval. Keeping the uncensored summary bit-identical to the release was preferred to making the two agree at the boundary, because every archived analysis is compared against it.

Extrapolation

extrapolate chooses the bound the estimate is censored at. It is read on the recorded predictor scale, the scale the data were supplied on and the scale bnec and nsec take x_range on. That is neither the scale crf() fits on nor the scale xform displays, so under crf(log(concentration)) the limit is a concentration and not a log concentration.

TRUE removes the bound at both ends. It is accepted only where every component of the reported estimate samples a NEC. An NSEC is read off a fitted curve and a curve cannot be evaluated on an infinite grid, so where any component is an NSEC — which includes the default bnec model set, because that set fits equations of both classes — TRUE is an error naming the finite form. For a single fit the class is the one recorded in ne_type, which takes both blocks of a joint two-block fit into account. For a model-averaged set it is read from each equation's name, which is where summary reads the label it prints, so the two cannot disagree about what the set is.

A finite limit applies to both classes, by a different route for each. The threshold components are compared against it, which requires no further computation because every draw of a sampled nec already has a value. The curve-read components are re-evaluated on a grid extended to it, through the x_range argument of nsec. That recomputes from the stored fit and needs no refit, but it does evaluate the curve once for each such equation, at a run time proportional to resolution. The re-evaluation reuses the number of grid points the fit stored unless resolution is given, so over a wider range the grid is proportionally coarser, and it reads its control at the lowest observed concentration, so its numbers can differ in the last digits from the stored summary.

Two requests re-evaluate nothing and return what extrapolate = FALSE returns: a limit equal to the current bounds, and any limit on a fit with no draw beyond either end, where every draw was identified inside the range the fit used and a wider grid has none left to identify. An object fitted before version 2.2.0 records nothing about which of its draws lie beyond the range, so it takes the second of those whatever its draws are, and extrapolate does nothing to it. Refit it, or rebuild the set with amend, to extrapolate from it.

A limit inside the prediction range is an error rather than a silent tightening, because it would report an estimate as censored at a value the fit had no trouble identifying. Narrow the range with x_range where the fit or the estimate is built instead.

Two constraints on the reach of an extrapolation are reported rather than corrected. Where the nec prior stored on the fit is itself bounded at the prediction range, the posterior holds no draw beyond that bound and a wider limit returns the same truncated posterior; a message states the bound. The default prior no longer bounds nec above, so this applies to a fit made before that change, or to a user prior that supplies a bound. The lower bound of 0 that a predictor supplied as a concentration still takes is reported by the other arm of the same message. And a curve-read component is measured from the control, so a lower limit below the lowest observed concentration extends the grid without extending the search, and those components stay censored at the control.

References

Fisher R, Fox DR (2023). Introducing the no significant effect concentration (NSEC). Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry, 42(9), 2019–2028. doi: 10.1002/etc.5610.

Fisher R, Fox DR, Negri AP, van Dam J, Flores F, Koppel D (2023). Methods for estimating no-effect toxicity concentrations in ecotoxicology. Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management. doi: 10.1002/ieam.4809.

Fox DR (2010). A Bayesian Approach for Determining the No Effect Concentration and Hazardous Concentration in Ecotoxicology. Ecotoxicology and Environmental Safety, 73(2), 123–131. doi: 10.1016/j.ecoenv.2009.09.012.

See also

bnec, nsec, summary

Examples

library(bayesnec)
data(manec_example)
nec(manec_example)
#> This bayesmanecfit contains smooth (ecx) models, which have no threshold parameter, so the returned estimate is a weighted mixture of NEC and NSEC draws -- the model-averaged N(S)EC rather than a NEC. See ?nec and summary(), which labels it.
#>       Q50      Q2.5     Q97.5 
#> 1.4503481 0.7487292 1.5273698 
#> attr(,"toxicity_estimate")
#> [1] "nec"
